analysis.one_liner: Lets banks own securities underwriting and brokerage affiliates, loosening the legal wall between banking and Wall Street.
analysis.headline: The bill never left the Senate Banking Committee: its sole sponsor had zero cosponsors, and it received no hearing or vote before the 101st Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would let bank holding companies own securities firms that underwrite and trade stocks and bonds, ending part of the Depression-era wall between insured banks and Wall Street. It would create new "diversified financial holding companies" and "safe bank holding companies" that escape many federal banking rules, speed up merger approvals, and preempt some state banking laws. It bundles in consumer protections — disclosure that securities are not FDIC-insured, limits on sharing customer data, and a ban on mergers between the largest banks and the largest securities firms. It died in committee without ever getting a hearing or a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Large bank holding companies gain the most: the power to own underwriting and brokerage affiliates, a new holding-company form that escapes Federal Reserve examination and capital rules, faster merger and acquisition approvals, and looser rules on shared management. Insurance companies gain a route into bank-affiliated conglomerates, and national banks gain authority to underwrite municipal revenue bonds and distribute investment company shares.

how_it_helps.text: Lets bank holding companies own "qualified affiliates" that underwrite, distribute, and deal in securities of any type and run brokerage and investment advisory businesses, overriding the 1933 Banking Act's separation of banks and securities firms.

Creates "diversified financial holding companies" — companies that control banks but are no longer legally bank holding companies — which may keep insurance underwriting and agency, real estate, and travel businesses, and are exempt from Federal Reserve examination, reporting, and capital requirements except in emergencies.

Creates "safe bank holding companies" that may hold shares of any company at all, as long as their bank holds investments as safe as its insured deposits; these banks get a lower deposit-insurance assessment and a special receivership process that pays any leftover proceeds to shareholders.

Speeds up deal-making: new nonbanking activities need only 60 days' notice instead of an application, and waiting periods after approval for holding-company acquisitions and bank mergers can shrink to as little as 5 days when no adverse comments come in.

Loosens the Depository Institution Management Interlocks Act: the ownership threshold for treating institutions as affiliated drops from 50% to 25%, failed or failing institutions get a five-year exemption, and grandfathered dual directorships are extended for five more years.

Shields domestic incumbents from some foreign competition: large foreign banks that acquire large U.S. investment banking organizations are barred from U.S. banking activities, and large foreign investment banks that acquire bank holding companies are barred from controlling securities affiliates.

Authorizes national banks without securities affiliates to underwrite municipal revenue bonds, sponsor unit investment trusts, and distribute investment company shares, and lets bankers' banks take outside capital investments to serve minority-owned banks.

analysis.who_pays: Bank depositors and the federal deposit insurance funds would stand behind larger, more complex conglomerates whose securities and insurance affiliates could run into trouble, with firewalls doing the protecting. Smaller securities firms would face new competition from bank giants. State governments would lose authority over banks: states could no longer bar bank-securities affiliations, and state-chartered banks with more than $250 million in deposits could not take on new state-authorized activities unless national banks have the same powers.
analysis.who_pays_short: Deposit insurance funds and smaller securities firms

drawbacks.text: It tears down part of the Glass-Steagall wall that since 1933 kept securities underwriting separate from insured deposits. The bill builds firewalls — credit restrictions between banks and securities affiliates, bans on interlocking directors, required disclosures — but those protections depend entirely on regulators enforcing them, and deposit insurance would end up backing bigger, riskier conglomerates.

It preempts state law: no state could prohibit a bank from affiliating with a securities affiliate, and no state could authorize a state-insured bank with more than $250 million in deposits to engage in any activity a national bank cannot, freezing out state-level consumer and banking protections.

Diversified financial holding companies and their nonbank subsidiaries would be exempt from Federal Reserve inspection, examination, reporting, and capital requirements, weakening oversight of companies that control insured banks.

It reduces scrutiny of concentration: merger waiting periods could drop to five days, interlock restrictions would cover far fewer combinations, and the Federal Reserve's power to review new activities would shrink to a notice-and-wait system.

For "safe banks," the special receivership pays net proceeds left after liquidation to shareholders rather than to the deposit insurance fund, a subtle shift of residual value away from the fund that backs depositors.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill is not a naked deregulation giveaway — it attaches real protections, including a ban on mergers between banks over $30 billion and securities firms over $15 billion, a customer-privacy rule barring the sharing of nonpublic customer information without consent, required disclosure that securities are not FDIC-insured, and a delay on equity underwriting until a separate vote in the next Congress. But its center of gravity is a large transfer of power to the biggest financial institutions: expanded securities powers, holding-company structures exempt from Fed oversight, faster mergers, and federal preemption of state authority. The benefits to ordinary customers are indirect and speculative; the risks — to deposit insurance and to regulatory control — are concrete. It never advanced, so none of this took effect.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in the Senate Banking Committee from the day it was introduced until the Congress ended, and never got a hearing, a markup, or a vote.

narrative.text: Senator Christopher Dodd of Connecticut introduced the bill on January 31, 1989; it was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs.
No other senator signed on — the bill ended with zero cosponsors from either party.

The committee took no further action. The full action history shows only the introduction and the referral, with no hearing, no committee vote, and no floor action before the 101st Congress ended on January 3, 1991.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The existing wall between banking and securities stood for the time being: incumbent securities firms kept underwriting to themselves rather than facing competition from bank giants, and large bank holding companies gained no new powers. The bill's consumer protections also never became law, but nothing was lost that customers then had.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Incumbent securities firms; the bank-securities wall stood

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken, and the bill had a single Democratic sponsor with zero cosponsors from either party, so no partisan split can be measured.

industries.note: The bill's core gift: banks over any size could own securities underwriting and brokerage affiliates, and new holding-company forms would escape Federal Reserve examination and capital rules while controlling insured banks. The same bill attaches firewalls, disclosure, and privacy rules that constrain how banks use those powers.

Brokerage, dealing, and corporate debt underwriting would open to bank affiliates, ending the firms' protected market — but mergers between banks over $30 billion and securities firms over $15 billion are banned, and equity underwriting is deferred to a future Congress, blunting the immediate hit.

Insurance is expressly excluded from the bill's definition of securities, and diversified financial holding companies may keep insurance underwriting and agency businesses — opening a route for insurers into bank-owning conglomerates with lighter Fed oversight.

industries.industry: Foreign banks and foreign investment banks
industries.note: Large foreign banks that acquire large U.S. investment banking organizations would be barred from U.S. banking activities, and the reverse combination is barred too — a protection for domestic incumbents dressed as a safety rule.

Small state banks with $250 million or less in deposits keep full freedom to use state-granted powers, but larger state banks could take on no new state-authorized activity unless national banks have it, and no state could block bank-securities affiliation.
